Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 92, verse 1–4:

Makkiyya, and its verses are 21. "It was revealed after al-A'la."
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Al-maghsha (that which covers): this may be the sun, from His saying ﴿And the night when it covers it﴾; or the day, from His saying ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾; or everything that conceals with its darkness, from His saying ﴿when it becomes dark﴾ (idha waqab). Tajalla (it became manifest): it appeared upon the removal of the darkness of the night.

Or it means: it became clear and was uncovered by the rising of the sun. ﴿And by Him who created﴾: al-Qadir (the Mighty in power), the Great in capability, who has power to create the male and the female from a single drop of water. It is also said: they are Adam, peace be upon him, and Hawwa (Eve).

In the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿and the male and the female﴾. Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿and He who created the male and the female﴾.

From al-Kisa'i: ﴿and what created the male and the female﴾ in the genitive (bi'l-jarr), taking it as a substitute (badal) for the place of ma (in ma khalaqa), meaning: "and what Allah created," i.e., "and the creature of Allah, the male and the female." The omission of the name of Allah is permitted because it is known through His being alone in creation, since there is no creator besides Him.

It is also said: Allah has not created any living creature that is neither male nor female. As for the khuntha (hermaphrodite), although its state is ambiguous to us, it is not ambiguous to Allah; it is known to be either male or female. So if someone swears by divorce that he did not meet, on his day, any male or female, and then he meets a khuntha whose state is ambiguous, he would be in breach (hanith), because in reality it is either male or female, even if it is ambiguous to us.

﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse﴾: shatta is the plural of shatit, i.e., your endeavours are varied and differing, and the explanation of their difference is given in what follows.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 92, verses 5–7:

﴿Then as for he who gives [in charity] and fears God, and affirms the best [reward]...﴾ — that is, he gives up the rights of his wealth, fears God and does not disobey Him, and affirms the best (al-husna): by "the best" (al-husna) is meant the best quality, which is faith. Or [it means] by the best creed (al-milla al-husna), which is the religion of Islam; or by the best reward (al-mathuba al-husna), which is Paradise.

﴿We shall indeed ease him toward ease.﴾ That is, We shall prepare him for it, from the ease (yusr) of the horse for riding when one saddles it and bridles it. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Everyone is made easy for what he was created for" [[Agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayhi) from the hadith of ʿImran ibn Husayn, and from the hadith of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

The meaning is: We will show kindness to him and grant him success, until obedience becomes the easiest and least burdensome of matters for him, from the words of God: ﴿Whoever Allah wishes to guide, He expands his breast to Islam.﴾ [[Mahmud said: "Facilitating for ease means creating kindnesses (al-alt̄af)... etc." Ahmad said: May he not extend his tongue here against the People of the Sunnah, but the truth has restrained him, so you see him distorting the statement, indeed nullifying it, for he burdens it with what it cannot bear; and upon his speech in such matters is the alarm of a frightened thief.]]

And as for he who is self-sufficient and renounces what is with God, as if he were independent of it, so he does not guard himself [against displeasure]. Or [it means]: he was self-sufficient through the desires of this world, [and thus was independent] of the bliss of Paradise, since it stands in contrast to "and guards [himself]."

"So We shall ease him toward the difficult [path]": that is, We shall forsake him and withhold from him the divine favours (alṭāf), so that obedience becomes the hardest and most burdensome thing for him, like the words of Allah: "He makes his breast constricted and tight, as if he were climbing up into the sky" [6:125]. Or He named the path of good "the easy" (al-yusrā), because its outcome is ease, and the path of evil "the difficult" (al-ʿusrā), because its outcome is hardship. Or by these two He meant the two paths of Paradise and Hell; that is: We shall guide them in the Hereafter to the two paths.

It has been said: these verses were revealed concerning Abu Bakr (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) and Abu Sufyan ibn Ḥarb.

"And what will his wealth avail him" [92:11]: an interrogative in the sense of denial, or a negation.

"When it fails" (taraddā): a verb of the form tafaʿʿala from radā (ruin), which means destruction; he means: death. Or "it fails" when he is placed in a pit, i.e., buried in the grave.

Or: "it fails" into the depths of Hell.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 92, verses 14–21:

Abu al-Zubayr read *tatalaza* (تتلظى). If you ask: how can He say ﴿None shall enter it but the most wretched﴾ and ﴿the most righteous shall be kept far from it﴾, when it is known that every wretched person will burn in it, and every pious person will be kept far from it? It is not restricted to the most wretched of the wretched to burn in it, nor to the most pious of the pious to be saved. And if you claim that *nar* (fire) is indefinite and means a specific fire reserved for the most wretched, then what will you do with His saying ﴿the most righteous shall be kept far from it﴾? It is known that the most sinful of the Muslims will be kept far from that specific fire, not only the most righteous of them. I say: the verse is about a comparison between a great figure among the polytheists and a great figure among the believers. He wanted to emphasise their two contradictory attributes, so He said "the most wretched" and made it exclusive to the burning, as if the Fire had been created only for him. And He said "the most righteous" and made it exclusive to salvation, as if Paradise had been created only for him. It is also said that they are Abu Jahl or Umayya ibn Khalaf, and that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) is the one who ﴿purifies himself (yatazakka)﴾, from *al-zaka'* (growth/purity), meaning he seeks to be pure before Allah, not intending show or reputation. Or it is from *tafa''ul* of *al-zakah* (giving alms).

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of *yatazakka*? I say: it has two aspects. If you make it a substitute (*badal*) for *yu'ti* (﴿who gives his wealth﴾), it has no place in i'rab, because it falls within the scope of the relative clause (*silah*), and relative clauses have no place in i'rab. If you make it a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yu'ti*, its place is in the accusative. ﴿Seeking the face of his Lord﴾ (*ibtigha'a wajhi rabbihi*) is an exception of a different kind from what precedes it, which is "favour" (*ni'mah*). The meaning is: no one has a favour with him except seeking the face of his Lord, like your saying: "There is no one in the house except a donkey."

Yahya ibn Wathhab read *illa ibtigha'u wajhi rabbihi* with the nominative case (*raf'*), according to the dialect of those who say: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." Bishr ibn Abi Hazim recited both dialects in his verse:

*Adahat khala'an qifaran la anisa biha*
*illa al-jaadhira wa'l-zhalaman takhtalif*

Its *khala'* (abandoned) and *qifar* (desolate) became, with no companion in it except the young gazelles and the ostriches that roam.

*Raqafat fiha qulusi kay tujawibani*
*aw bi-khabari'l-rasmi 'anhum ayyata 'nsarafu*

I halted my young she-camel there so that it might answer me, or with news of the traces, where they went away.

These lines are by Bishr ibn Abi Hazim. *Khala'ya* is the plural of *khaliyah*, meaning empty. *Al-jaadhira* and *al-zhalaman* are an exception that is disconnected (*munqati'*), because they are not included among companions. Both have been transmitted in the accusative as exception, and in the nominative as substitution for the hidden pronoun in *khabar*, as is the dialect of Tamim. *Al-jaadhir* are the young of wild cattle. It is also transmitted as *al-jawazi*, which are gazelles that have been content with eating spring pasture rather than drinking water. *Al-zhaliman* are the young of ostriches, or the ostrich itself. *Al-qulus* are young she-camels with firm flesh. The pronoun in *fiha* refers back to the abodes, and so does the pronoun in *tujawibani*. *Al-rasm* means the traces of the abodes. *Ayyah* is an interrogative noun in the accusative, used adverbially because it is cut off from its genitive complement, meaning: their resolve and intention turned them away. The *rasm* is likened to a rational being by way of metaphor (*makniyyah*), so news is attributed to it by imagination (*takhyil*), and likewise the abode and its answering.

And the saying of the poet:

*Wa baldatin laysa biha anis*
*illa al-ya'afir wa illa al-'is*

Many a time we leave the dwelling, O Lamis, where the loud-voiced lion lives.

*Wa baldatin laysa biha anis*
*illa al-ya'afir wa illa al-'is*

This is by Amir ibn al-Harith, famous as Jiran al-Ud. Lamis is a woman's name. *Al-jurus* means one with a loud voice. *Baldah* is in the genitive, governed by the implied *rubba* after the conjunction *wa*, meaning: we may leave the dwelling empty of its people by killing them, or because we departed from them. *Al-ya'afir* is in the nominative, as a substitution for *anis*, according to the dialect of Tamim in exception after negation. The second *illa* is an emphasis for the first. *Al-ya'afir* is the plural of *ya'fur*, a creature the size of a kid, of ash colour. It is also said to be a gazelle of that kind, and it is also said to be the young of a wild cow. *Al-'is* are the white gazelles or camels, the plural of *a'is* or *'aysa'*. *Al-'aysa'* is also the female locust, whose whiteness is mixed with reddish tint.

It is also permissible for *ibtigha'a wajhi rabbihi* to be an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) according to the meaning, because the sense of the speech is: he does not give his wealth except seeking the face of his Lord, not as a requital for a favour. ﴿And he will surely be well-pleased﴾ is a promise of the reward that will please him and gladden his eye.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah *Wa'l-Layl* (Surah al-Layl), Allah will give him until he is content, will protect him from hardship, and will make ease easy for him."

(Narrated by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.)

It is not restricted to the most wretched of the wretched to burn in it, nor to the most pious of the pious to be saved. And if you claim that *nar* (fire) is indefinite and means a specific fire reserved for the most wretched, then what will you do with His saying ﴿the most righteous shall be kept far from it﴾? It is known that the most sinful of the Muslims will be kept far from that specific fire, not only the most righteous of them. I say: the verse is about a comparison between a great figure among the polytheists and a great figure among the believers. He wanted to emphasise their two contradictory attributes, so He said "the most wretched" and made it exclusive to the burning, as if the Fire had been created only for him. And He said "the most righteous" and made it exclusive to salvation, as if Paradise had been created only for him. It is also said that they are Abu Jahl or Umayya ibn Khalaf, and that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) is the one who ﴿purifies himself (yatazakka)﴾, from *al-zaka'* (growth/purity), meaning he seeks to be pure before Allah, not intending show or reputation. Or it is from *tafa''ul* of *al-zakah* (giving alms).

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of *yatazakka*? I say: it has two aspects. If you make it a substitute (*badal*) for *yu'ti* (﴿who gives his wealth﴾), it has no place in i'rab, because it falls within the scope of the relative clause (*silah*), and relative clauses have no place in i'rab. If you make it a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yu'ti*, its place is in the accusative. ﴿Seeking the face of his Lord﴾ (*ibtigha'a wajhi rabbihi*) is an exception of a different kind from what precedes it, which is "favour" (*ni'mah*). The meaning is: no one has a favour with him except seeking the face of his Lord, like your saying: "There is no one in the house except a donkey."

Yahya ibn Wathhab read *illa ibtigha'u wajhi rabbihi* with the nominative case (*raf'*), according to the dialect of those who say: "There is no one in the house except a donkey." Bishr ibn Abi Hazim recited both dialects in his verse:

*Adahat khala'an qifaran la anisa biha*
*illa al-jaadhira wa'l-zhalaman takhtalif*

Its *khala'* (abandoned) and *qifar* (desolate) became, with no companion in it except the young gazelles and the ostriches that roam.

*Raqafat fiha qulusi kay tujawibani*
*aw bi-khabari'l-rasmi 'anhum ayyata 'nsarafu*

I halted my young she-camel there so that it might answer me, or with news of the traces, where they went away.

These lines are by Bishr ibn Abi Hazim. *Khala'ya* is the plural of *khaliyah*, meaning empty. *Al-jaadhira* and *al-zhalaman* are an exception that is disconnected (*munqati'*), because they are not included among companions. Both have been transmitted in the accusative as exception, and in the nominative as substitution for the hidden pronoun in *khabar*, as is the dialect of Tamim. *Al-jaadhir* are the young of wild cattle. It is also transmitted as *al-jawazi*, which are gazelles that have been content with eating spring pasture rather than drinking water. *Al-zhaliman* are the young of ostriches, or the ostrich itself. *Al-qulus* are young she-camels with firm flesh. The pronoun in *fiha* refers back to the abodes, and so does the pronoun in *tujawibani*. *Al-rasm* means the traces of the abodes. *Ayyah* is an interrogative noun in the accusative, used adverbially because it is cut off from its genitive complement, meaning: their resolve and intention turned them away. The *rasm* is likened to a rational being by way of metaphor (*makniyyah*), so news is attributed to it by imagination (*takhyil*), and likewise the abode and its answering.

And the saying of the poet:

*Wa baldatin laysa biha anis*
*illa al-ya'afir wa illa al-'is*

Many a time we leave the dwelling, O Lamis, where the loud-voiced lion lives.

*Wa baldatin laysa biha anis*
*illa al-ya'afir wa illa al-'is*

This is by Amir ibn al-Harith, famous as Jiran al-Ud. Lamis is a woman's name. *Al-jurus* means one with a loud voice. *Baldah* is in the genitive, governed by the implied *rubba* after the conjunction *wa*, meaning: we may leave the dwelling empty of its people by killing them, or because we departed from them. *Al-ya'afir* is in the nominative, as a substitution for *anis*, according to the dialect of Tamim in exception after negation. The second *illa* is an emphasis for the first. *Al-ya'afir* is the plural of *ya'fur*, a creature the size of a kid, of ash colour. It is also said to be a gazelle of that kind, and it is also said to be the young of a wild cow. *Al-'is* are the white gazelles or camels, the plural of *a'is* or *'aysa'*. *Al-'aysa'* is also the female locust, whose whiteness is mixed with reddish tint.

It is also permissible for *ibtigha'a wajhi rabbihi* to be an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) according to the meaning, because the sense of the speech is: he does not give his wealth except seeking the face of his Lord, not as a requital for a favour. ﴿And he will surely be well-pleased﴾ is a promise of the reward that will please him and gladden his eye.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah *Wa'l-Layl* (Surah al-Layl), Allah will give him until he is content, will protect him from hardship, and will make ease easy for him."

(Narrated by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.)
